help.title: Tolerance Interval Capability
help.body:
Description
Tolerance Interval Capability answers the question: "Given n measurements, what mean-to-limit margin do I need so that at least p × 100% of the population clears the spec limit, with (1−α) × 100% confidence?"

What is the k-factor?
The k-factor is a sample-size-aware safety multiplier. It tells you how many standard deviations your process mean must sit away from the limit per unit of standard deviation, accounting for the uncertainty introduced by having only n measurements. If you had infinitely many measurements you would only need a z-score (e.g. z = 3.09 for p = 0.999); with a finite sample, k > z and grows as n shrinks.

Mathematically, k comes from the non-central t-distribution:
  k(n, p, γ) = tν, δ, γ / √n
where ν = n − 1 (degrees of freedom), δ = √n · Φ⁻¹(p) (non-centrality parameter), and γ is the confidence level.

k-Factor computation methods
The k-factor method affects numerical precision and speed; all methods converge to the same value as n grows large. Change only when matching another tool's output.
  • WBE (default) — Wald-Brookner-Edwards approximation. Fast, accurate for all n, and the only method available for two-sided intervals in R's tolerance package. Recommended in nearly all cases.
  • EXACT — Exact non-central t inversion via numerical integration. Highest precision for one-sided intervals with n ≤ 100. For two-sided intervals or n > 100, the tolerance package silently falls back to WBE, so results will be identical to WBE in those cases.
  • HE — Howe's (1969) first approximation. Widely cited in early tolerance-interval literature; slightly less accurate than WBE at small n.
  • HE2 — Howe's second approximation. A refined version of HE; marginally more accurate at very small n.
  • ELL — Ellison's (2000) approximation. Derived for calibration contexts; behaves similarly to WBE for most engineering use.
  • KM — Krishnamoorthy-Mathew (2009) method. Based on a generalized pivotal quantity; accurate for both one- and two-sided intervals.
  • OCT — Odeh-Owen (one-sided) / exact Clopper-Pearson (two-sided). Uses tables originally published by Odeh & Owen; may give slightly different results at extreme p or confidence values.
Note: When Both (two-sided) is selected, the method dropdown above is ignored — R's tolerance package always uses WBE for two-sided intervals regardless of which method is chosen. The dropdown only affects one-sided (Lower/Upper) calculations.

Two-sided formula (Both mode only)
When "Both" is selected, two statistically valid approaches exist for computing k. Note: When Lower or Upper is selected, this radio button is ignored — only the method dropdown above applies.

Bonferroni / K.factor(side=2) — Default. Applies a Bonferroni correction so that both tolerance limits (lower and upper) simultaneously achieve the stated coverage. More conservative (larger k). Statistically rigorous; recommended for formal qualification and compliance testing (ASTM E2810, ISO 16269-6).

Split-NCT (per-tail) — Uses the one-sided NCT formula with an effective probability peff = 1 − (1−p)/2 per tail (e.g. p=0.99 → peff=0.995). This is the method used by some industry tools, automotive quality templates, and some aerospace procedures. Less conservative (smaller k) because it guarantees per-tail coverage independently rather than joint simultaneous coverage. Use this option when you need to reconcile results with an existing tool e.g. Excel based formulas.

Example (n=24, p=0.99, confidence=90%, Both):
  Bonferroni k = 4.28  |  Split-NCT k = 3.27

Outputs
Capability C — ratio of available margin to required margin:
C = (x̄ − LSL) / (k · s)  [lower]  |  C = (USL − x̄) / (k · s)  [upper]  |  C = min(x̄ − LSL, USL − x̄) / (k · s)  [both]
PASS if C ≥ 1.0; FAIL if C < 1.0.

Margin to spec limit — physical distance between the tolerance limit and the specification limit, reported alongside each TL in the console and Capability Summary table:
  Margin above LSL = TL_lower − LSL  [lower or both]
  Margin below USL = USL − TL_upper  [upper or both]
A positive margin means the tolerance limit clears the spec; a negative margin means it does not. Useful for understanding how much cushion (or shortfall) exists in physical units.

Cpk bridge — translates the result into familiar Cpk language:
Cpk = (x̄ − LSL) / (σ_div · s)  [lower]
Cpk = (USL − x̄) / (σ_div · s)  [upper]
Cpk = min(x̄ − LSL, USL − x̄) / (σ_div · s)  [both]
Minimum required Cpk = k / σ_div  (threshold derived from the k-factor).
Capability difference = Cpk − minimum required Cpk (positive = margin above threshold).

Two-sided interval verdict (Both mode only) — PASS if both TL_lower ≥ LSL AND TL_upper ≤ USL simultaneously; reported separately from the C verdict.

Capability chart — shows the process distribution (bell curve) with the spec limit(s), tolerance limit(s) (TL), and process mean overlaid. The spec limit line is labeled LSL in Lower and Both modes and USL in Upper mode, matching the role of the limit value L in each mode.
The orange shaded region represents the fraction of the population that falls beyond the tolerance limit — i.e., the unprotected (1 − p) tail. It is always shaded orange (not pass/fail colored) and always shaded from the TL outward toward the plot edge, so it remains visible even when the process is well-centered. A smaller orange region means a higher reliability: more of the population is inside the tolerance limit. At p = 0.999 the tail is 0.1% of the population; at p = 0.90 it is 10%, so the orange region is visibly larger at lower reliability settings.

Inputs
n — total number of individual measurements (integer ≥ 2). When a dataset variable is selected, n is computed automatically from non-missing observations.
Confidence — statistical confidence in the tolerance statement (default 0.95).
Reliability — minimum fraction of the population that must clear the limit (default 0.999).
Limit value L — the specification (LSL for lower/both; USL for upper mode).
USL — upper specification limit (required when Both is selected).
Sigma divisor — denominator for Cpk (default 3; use 6 for Six Sigma targets).
Observed x̄ and s — optional; supply these (or select a dataset variable) to compute Capability Calculated and see whether the process passes.

Assumptions and references
Assumes the characteristic is normally distributed. Equivalent to the normal tolerance interval in ASTM E2810 and ISO 16269-6. k-factor computed via R's tolerance package (Young 2010).
